question: A news site drew US drug overdose deaths in red, from 2015 to 2023. The line seems to fall. Where's the trick?
answer: In the axis: zero sits at the top, so every rise is drawn as a fall. Reuters did this in 2014 with Florida gun deaths, styled as dripping blood, and many readers saw a drop. Right way up, overdose deaths doubled in seven years, driven by opioids, the painkillers' family, now mostly street fentanyl.
move: Before reading a slope, find where zero sits on the axis.
ask: Do I check which way an axis runs before deciding things got better or worse?

scene.headline: Overdose deaths in America
scene.label: US overdose deaths, thousands
scene.found: Yes: zero is at the top, so the line drops as deaths climb.
scene.miss: That part is fair. Check which way the axis numbers run.

misses.headline: A neutral title. The drawing is what says 'falling'.
misses.marks: The line is true to its axis. Read the axis itself.

scene.name: Upside-down axis
scene.lesson: Up is not always more. Find zero on the axis before you read which way a line goes.

reference: Garnett & Miniño, Drug Overdose Deaths in the United States, 2003–2023, NCHS Data Brief No. 522, 2024; Chan, Gun deaths in Florida, Reuters graphic, February 2014
